questions.title: What is the specific algorithmic difference between Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) and standard Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) regarding the value function?
questions.question_body:
The paper introduces GRPO as a variant of PPO that removes the critic model to save memory. However, I am struggling to understand the mathematical substitution they make.

In the equation for the PPO surrogate objective, there is a term $A_t$ representing advantage, which is calculated using Generalized Advantage Estimation (GAE): 
$$A_t = \sum_{r_{\ge t}} \gamma^{k} (R_k - V_{\psi})$$

Since GRPO removes the learned value function $V_{\psi}$ entirely, how exactly does it re-derive the "baseline" for this calculation? The text mentions using "average reward of multiple sampled outputs" as a baseline. Does it simply replace the scalar $V_{\psi}$ with a relative mean across a group $ ar{r}$? Specifically, in Equation (\ref{eq:GRPO-obj}), how are the individual advantages $\\hat{A}_{i,t}$ normalized without one token knowing about rewards for other tokens that haven't been generated yet?

questions.title: Why does training DeepSeekMath-Base on code tokens prior to math tokens improve mathematical reasoning without tool use?
questions.question_body:
The paper makes a strong claim in Section 6.1 regarding code training, specifically that it boosts math reasoning on GSM8K and MATH *without* requiring external toolkits or coding execution. This seems counter-intuitive to me because I expected code training only to help if the model could access Python libraries.

Reading Section 5.3 on "Code Training Benefits Mathematical Reasoning", they note:
1. Code training improves program-aided reasoning (using tools).
2. Code training *also* improves non-tool (step-by-step text) reasoning.

Can someone clarify the intuition here? Is there a causal link between understanding Python syntax (likely seen in Common Crawl code data) and better logical deduction when solving word problems like $x + y = z$ purely with text? Or is it possible that they meant code training helps with *writing down* the logic efficiently rather than solving it per se?
